svg.title: Why wireless makes layer 2 a first class citizen: the AP to WLC path, what roaming requires and the design answers
svg.desc: A horizontal chain of AP, access switch, WLC and core, with the note that the client's VLAN is mapped at the WLC or the AP but must exist on every switch the user can walk to, which is why wireless forces layer 2 across closets even when every wired port is routed. Two panels follow. What roaming requires: the same subnet and gateway during the roam, the same mobility domain across controllers, fast transition for voice, and a CAPWAP path that does not hairpin the whole campus, with the warning that cross-controller roaming without a mobility domain costs a re-authentication and one to three seconds of silence. Design answers in order of cost: one closet per subnet with AP local switching, stretched VLANs only for SSIDs that must roam, a fabric with an anycast gateway, and a controller cluster with a tested mobility domain. A footer ties PoE budgets to the same decision.
svg.text: Wireless puts layer 2 back in charge
An AP is a layer 2 bridge with a roaming requirement, so the VLAN has to follow the user across closets.
AP
bridge, 802.11
Access switch
PoE + trunk
WLC
CAPWAP, mobility
Core / DC
same VLAN?
the client's VLAN is mapped at the WLC or at the AP, but it must exist on every switch the user can walk to
that is why wireless forces layer 2 across closets even when every wired port is routed
WHAT ROAMING ACTUALLY REQUIRES
- same subnet and gateway during the roam
- same mobility domain across controllers
- fast transition (802.11r/k/v) for voice
- the AP's CAPWAP path must not hairpin the whole campus
cross-controller roaming without a mobility domain = re-auth, 1-3 s of silence
DESIGN ANSWERS, IN ORDER OF COST
- one closet = one subnet, AP local switching (cheapest)
- stretched VLAN only for the SSIDs that must roam
- fabric / EVPN anycast gateway (most expensive, no L2 stretch
- controller cluster with a mobility domain, tested roaming
and a voice test: walk the stairs while on a call, then read the logs
PoE is part of the same decision: 802.3at 30 W for Wi-Fi 6, 802.3bt 60-90 W for 6E/7, budgeted with 20% headroom - see the capacity figure.
